title: sleep
hook: deep sleep leaves nothing to tell at breakfast; the Brihadaranyaka describes it anyway, with a falcon

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep and the dream: the dreamer self-lit, making chariots and rivers where there are none. This morning, did you stay with one dream image, or the dark, before the phone? Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

Deep sleep is the one part of the night with nothing to report. No dream to tell over breakfast. No story, no scene, no plot that falls apart as you try to explain it. Just a gap, and then the alarm. A gap seems an odd thing to teach. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tries anyway. Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, has walked through waking and through dreams. Now he goes one step further down, and to describe it, he reaches for a bird. Today: the sleep with no dreams in it.
screen: `NOTHING TO REPORT.` → `A GAP, THEN THE ALARM.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the bird, in paraphrase. A falcon, or an eagle, has been flying around in the open sky. It's tired. So it folds its wings and drops down to its nest. In the same way, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, he wants nothing at all and sees no dream. Then Yajnavalkya says something stranger. There, a father is not a father. A mother is not a mother. The worlds are not worlds, the gods not gods, the Vedas not Vedas. A thief is not a thief. He is untouched by good and untouched by evil, the text says, for he has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart. Turn it a few ways. First, the folded wings. The falcon isn't defeated. It flew all day; that's what falcons do. Folding the wings is just the other half of flying. Second, the roles. Every name a person carries in the daytime, parent, worker, friend, the one with a reputation, even the one with a past, is set down in deep sleep. Not erased. Set down. In the morning they're all picked back up. Third, the sorrows of the heart. The text doesn't say grief is cured. It says only that, in that state, the sleeper has crossed over it: a nightly crossing, made without any effort at all. One more turn, for honesty. Yajnavalkya isn't saying the goal of life is to sleep well. Deep sleep, for him, is a clue: a nightly taste of being without wanting. Another Upanishad, the Mandukya, lines up waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and points past all of them. That's a road for other days.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS` · `A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER` · `THE SORROWS OF THE HEART, CROSSED` · `A CLUE, NOT THE GOAL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fold the wings. Sit or lie comfortably, and let the breath slow. Then name, silently, one role you carried today. Parent, maybe. Worker. Friend. Student. The one who has to answer. With the next breath out, set it down beside you, not thrown away, just put down. Then the next one. When there are no more names, rest for a while in whatever is left. If you pray, you can rest in prayer there. The bell holds the time.
Sleep. In deep sleep, the Brihadaranyaka says, a person wants nothing, sees no dream, and has crossed the sorrows of the heart, like a falcon folding its wings. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Tonight, lying down, set down one role at a time, the way a falcon folds one wing and then the other. Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers study deep, dreamless sleep, sushupti, beside waking and dreaming, and read Yajnavalkya's falcon as a picture of the self at rest.

fork.setup: you're the falcon. you've flown the open sky all day and you're tired. what do you do?
options: fold your wings and go down to your nest.
fork.reveal: the falcon folds its wings and goes to its nest. so a person hurries, the text says, toward the sleep where he wants nothing and sees no dream.

original.note: Sanskrit sushupti: deep, dreamless sleep, the name later Vedanta teachers give the state this passage describes.

trapdoor: what you thought: deep sleep is a blank, nothing to say about it.
what it means: for Yajnavalkya, it's the falcon's nest: wanting nothing, no dream, the sorrows of the heart crossed over.
what a scholar hears: a father not a father, a thief not a thief, untouched by good and by evil: every daytime name set down.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.19 (the tired falcon or eagle folds its wings and goes to its nest; the sleeper desires no desire, sees no dream)

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.22 (a father is not a father, a mother not a mother, worlds not worlds, gods not gods, Vedas not Vedas, a thief not a thief; untouched by good and evil; crossed all sorrows of the heart)
Mandukya Upanishad 3–7 (waking, dreaming, deep sleep and the fourth)

notes: Brihadaranyaka 4.3.19: confirm the falcon (shyena) or eagle (suparna) paraphrase and 'na kanchana kamam kamayate na kanchana svapnam pashyati'.
4.3.22: confirm the list as paraphrased and 'crossed all the sorrows of the heart' (tirno hi tada sarvan chokan hridayasya bhavati).
Editor pass: removed the unsourced generalization about what grieving people report; 'later teachers' now names the cited Mandukya; the hook no longer tells the listener what they'd think.
'A few clear seconds before remembering a loss' is an everyday picture, not a claim from the text; phrased as 'people who are grieving sometimes speak of', not as the listener's experience.
'Later teachers lined up waking, dreaming and deep sleep and pointed past them' refers to the Mandukya's turiya; kept without counts.
Sushupti is a later technical term; the note says so.
